response.answer: Incorporate Bayesian posterior probability or confidence intervals for precision into progression criteria instead of a binary cutoff. results.content: Bayesian estimation is defined as a statistical method where the parameters of a linear model are treated as random variables, with prior probability distributions reflecting the investigator's prior knowledge. where *P*(*x*̃) is known as the prior, as it conveys the prior information available about noise-free variables, is the posterior, representing the probability distribution of the noise-free variables after the set of measurements has been collected, *P(x)* is the probability distribution for the measurements (which can be disregarded from the analysis, as it is independent of *x*̃, the free variables of the Bayesian rectification problem), and stands for the noise’s probability distribution, also equal to the likelihood of the measurements when the noise-free signal equals a given value of *x*̃. By using the prescribed prior distribution and probability distribution of the data (which is defined by the assumed data model), MCMC methods allow for simulating a sequence of parameter values which theory dictates have the correct distribution, which is to say, they are a sample from the target posterior distribution. In a Bayesian setting, all the information about *θ* from the observed data and from the prior knowledge is contained in the posterior distribution, π(*θ***|***x*). All inferences from Bayesian methods are based on the posterior probability distribution of the parameter *θ*. results.title: How to choose prior in Bayesian parameter estimation - Cross Validated
results.content: # How to choose prior in Bayesian parameter estimation. And for MAP and Bayes approach, we need to pick priors for parameters, right? Say I have this model $p(x|\alpha,\beta)$, in which $\alpha,\beta$ are parameters, in order to do the estimation using MAP or Bayes, I read in the book that we'd better *pick a conjugate prior $p(\alpha,\beta)$*, which is a **joint** probability of $\alpha,\beta$, right? first and foremost, you should make sure that your priors represent your prior beliefs about the distribution of the parameters $\endgroup$. * $\begingroup$ So I could just pick priors respectively for the parameters,right ? * $\begingroup$ How to show that a Beta distribution is a conjugate prior for a Binomial distribution youtu.be/Q4HFHXs2m7Y $\endgroup$. As stated in comment, the prior distribution represents prior beliefs about the distribution of the parameters. * use your intuitive understanding of these beliefs to propose a given prior distribution and check if it really fits your purpose and that it is not to sensitive to arbitrary choices (performing a robustness or sensibility analysis). * sometimes such choices are impossible or quite difficult to derive and in this case, you can try to choose among one of the many "generic" weakly informative prior (e.g. uniform shrinkage distribution for scale parameters of hierarchical model or $g$-prior for gaussian regression). * take care that your posterior is integrable almost everywhere (or proper), which is always true if you use an integrable prior (see Does the Bayesian posterior need to be a proper distribution? And this link give s a good summary of how to incorporate a prior to Bayesian inference for a binomial distribution. * $\begingroup$ A minor elaboration: A proper prior represents *a* consistent set of beliefs about the parameters. The problem is that if you choose non-conjugate priors, you cannot make exact Bayesian inference (simply put, you cannot derive a close-form posterior). 0") Best probability density function to use for the prior of a variance parameter in Bayesian inference. 4") Conjugate priors for Gamma distribution of unknown $\alpha$ and $\beta$. 5") Bayesian estimation by sampling the prior? 3") [Bayesian estimation of iid sample from Uniform$[0,\theta]$ and a Pareto$(\alpha,\beta)$ prior for $\theta$](/questions/606976/bayesian-estimation-of-iid-sample-from-uniform0-theta-and-a-pareto-alpha).
